1 Filling gaps in lecture notes (10% pts)

Consider the regression model \[ Y = f(X) + \epsilon, \] where \(\operatorname{E}(\epsilon) = 0\).

1.1 Optimal regression function

Show that the choice \[ f_{\text{opt}}(X) = \operatorname{E}(Y | X) \] minimizes the mean squared prediction error \[ \operatorname{E}\{[Y - f(X)]^2\}, \] where the expectations averages over variations in both \(X\) and \(Y\). (Hint: condition on \(X\).)

1.2 Bias-variance trade-off

Given an estimate \(\hat f\) of \(f\), show that the test error at a \(x_0\) can be decomposed as \[ \operatorname{E}\{[y_0 - \hat f(x_0)]^2\} = \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(\hat f(x_0)) + [\operatorname{Bias}(\hat f(x_0))]^2}_{\text{MSE of } \hat f(x_0) \text{ for estimating } f(x_0)} + \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)}_{\text{irreducible}}, \] where the expectation averages over the variability in \(y_0\) and \(\hat f\).

3 ISL Exercise 2.4.4 (10% pts)

You will now think of some real-life applications for statistical learning.

  1. Describe three real-life applications in which classification might be useful.Describe the response, as well as the predictors. Is the goal of each application inference or prediction? Explain your answer.

One useful example would be email spam detection. Having the ability to quickly sort through important emails and emails that will waste your time is a very practical for daily time management.

The response in this case would be if the email itself is classified as spam or not. This could be a binary classification 1 = spam, 0 = not spam.

The predictors in this case would be features in the emails themselves such as email address, certain keywords that advertisers use, metadata of the email itself (for example what time the email was sent).

The goal in this case is prediction. The model will be introduced to new emails constantly and will need to make a new prediction if the incoming email is classified as spam or not, based on prior data patterns or other parameters set by the model.

Another real-life application would be medical diagnosis. Certain cells in the human body could be classified as cancerous or benign. This is another example of binary classification.

The response in this case could be “cancerous” or benign”

Predictors would be various bio-statistical data pertaining to each patient such as age, blood levels, certain diets, concentration of exotic substances (radiation, carcinogenic chemicals)

The goal in this case would again be prediction. We are taking trained data from previous patients that had confirmed classified cases of cancer or not, and then applying that learned model to new patient data to predict if this new patient has cancer or not.

Last example given here could be in evaluating the effectiveness of a new drug.

The response would be whether or not a patient has improved or not improved.

Predictors in this case could be the dosage amount, overall health of the patients and other various demographics of the individuals that participate in the placebo (control) group vs that of the new drug (experimental) group.

This would be an example of an inference. We are taking in new data and making an inference on how statistically significant is the new drug performing. We are not making any predictive outcomes for individuals that take this drug.

  1. Describe three real-life applications in which regression might be useful. Describe the response, as well as the predictors. Is the goal of each application inference or prediction? Explain your answer.

One example that was brought up in our lectures was advertising and the effect it has on sales.

The response here would the be sales figures themselves (how many units were sold, gross revenue).

The predictors in this case would be the amount spent on advertising, the advertising contents (what is being advertised and how), what time of the year it is (some products will sell better in the Winter for example), and the price of the product itself.

The goal here could depend on what we are trying to achieve. If we want to know how well a future product will do, we could be making a regression prediction. If we want to understand how well advertising expenditure effects previous products we would be doing a inference on that relationship (for example advertising revue vs sales revenue).

Another real-life example would be in housing prices.

The response would be the price of the house.

Predictors would be various features of that house such as number of bedrooms, square footage, location, or other special extensions of the house like a pool.

The goal here is prediction. We are aiming to predict the selling price of a house based on certain criteria.

Final example here would be for analyzing employee salaries.

The response would be the employee salary.

Predictors would be years of experience, education level, job position, location, an performance statistics if available.

The goal here is to infer how various factors influence an employee’s salary. We are aiming to understand the relationship between various factors instead of trying to make a specific prediction of an individual’s salary.

  1. Describe three real-life applications in which cluster analysis might be useful.

One real-life example would be Image segmentation in computer vision projects. Often times we want to divide an image into different segments to help identify what is in a picture for example. There are a wide range of useful reasons to do this, one quick example is diagnosing diseases based of x-ray images or MRI scans by quickly sorting what is ordinary in the scan and what is abnormal.

We could apply cluster analysis to customers in marketing as well. Grouping customers into clusters based of purchasing behavior or demographics can help companies identify various types of customers such as frequent shoppers or one-time buyers. These companies can than look into specifics per group and adjust various tactics such as targeted marking.

Final example could be used for streaming services. Viewers of certain streaming services like Netflix can be clustered based on factors like minutes watched per day, total viewing sessions per week, or number of unique shows watched per month. These users can be clustered into high or low usage users and then the streaming companies can focus specific marketing strategies on the clusters that are more likely to return the most revenue.

5 ISL Exercise 3.7.3 (20% pts)

Suppose we have a data set with five predictors, X1 = GPA, X2 = IQ, X3 = Level (1 for College and 0 for High School), X4 = Interaction between GPA and IQ, and X5 = Interaction between GPA and Level. The response is starting salary after graduation (in thousands of dollars). Suppose we use least squares to ft the model, and get βˆ0 = 50, βˆ1 = 20, βˆ2 = 0.07, βˆ3 = 35, βˆ4 = 0.01, βˆ5 = −10.

  1. Which answer is correct, and why?
  1. For a fixed value of IQ and GPA, college graduates earn more, on average, than high school graduates provided that the GPA is high enough.

Because there is a high positive coefficient attracted to the level of education, our model suggests that the level of education (being in college) is a strong predictor in having a higher salary (from βˆ3 = 35). The negative coefficient (βˆ5 = −10) for the interaction between GPA and level of education, suggests that a certain level of GPA is needed for the correlation of salary and education level to be visualized.

  1. Predict the salary of a college graduate with IQ of 110 and a GPA of 4.0.

\[ Salary=50+20⋅GPA+0.07⋅IQ+35⋅Level+0.01⋅(GPA×IQ)+(−10)⋅(GPA×Level)\]

Plug in values \[ Level = 1, GPA = 4.0, IQ = 110\]

\[ Salary=50+80+7.7+35+4.4−40=137.1 \]

  1. True or false: Since the coefficient for the GPA/IQ interaction term is very small, there is very little evidence of an interaction effect. Justify your answer.

False. We would need to perform a null-hypothesis test or report the standard error on this coefficient in order to evaluate how significant this value is.

6 ISL Exercise 3.7.15 (20% pts)

This problem involves the Boston data set, which we saw in the lab for this chapter. We will now try to predict per capita crime rate using the other variables in this data set. In other words, per capita crime rate is the response, and the other variables are the predictors.

  1. For each predictor, ft a simple linear regression model to predict the response. Describe your results. In which of the models is there a statistically significant association between the predictor and the response? Create some plots to back up your assertions.
# Load the necessary libraries
library(MASS)

# Get the list of predictors (exclude 'CRIM' from the dataset)
predictors <- setdiff(names(Boston), "crim")

# Loop through each predictor and fit the linear model
models <- lapply(predictors, function(predictor) {
  lm(crim ~ get(predictor), data = Boston)
})

# Display summaries for each model
model_summaries <- lapply(models, summary)
print(model_summaries)

  1. How do your results from (a) compare to your results from (b)?

Create a plot displaying the univariate regression coefficients from (a) on the x-axis, and the multiple regression coefficients from (b) on the y-axis. That is, each predictor is displayed as a single point in the plot.

# Step 1: Fit the univariate regression models and extract coefficients
predictors <- setdiff(names(Boston), "crim")  # Exclude the response variable 'CRIM'

# Fit univariate models and extract coefficients
univariate_coefs <- sapply(predictors, function(predictor) {
  model <- lm(crim ~ get(predictor), data = Boston)
  coef(model)[2]  # Extract the coefficient for the predictor (ignoring the intercept)
})

# Step 2: Fit the multiple regression model
multiple_model <- lm(crim ~ ., data = Boston)

# Extract the coefficients from the multiple regression model
multiple_coefs <- coef(multiple_model)[-1]  # Exclude the intercept

# Step 3: Create a data frame for plotting
coef_data <- data.frame(
  predictor = predictors,
  univariate = univariate_coefs,
  multiple = multiple_coefs
)

# Step 4: Create the plot
ggplot(coef_data, aes(x = univariate, y = multiple)) +
  geom_point() +  # Add points for each predictor
  geom_text(aes(label = predictor), hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.5) +  # Add labels with predictor names
  labs(title = "Univariate vs. Multiple Regression Coefficients",
       x = "Univariate Coefficients (Part a)",
       y = "Multiple Regression Coefficients (Part b)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Its coefficient in a simple linear regression model is shown on the x-axis, and its coefficient estimate in the multiple linear regression model is shown on the y-axis.

  1. Is there evidence of non-linear association between any of the predictors and the response? To answer this question, for each predictor X, ft a model of the form Y = β0 + β1X + β2X2 + β3X3 + ϵ.
# Get the list of predictors (exclude 'CRIM' from the dataset)
predictors <- setdiff(names(Boston), "crim")

# Step 1: Fit a quadratic model for each predictor and extract coefficients
quadratic_models <- lapply(predictors, function(predictor) {
  lm(crim ~ get(predictor) + I(get(predictor)^2), data = Boston)
})

# Step 2: Display summaries for each quadratic model to check the significance of the quadratic term
quadratic_summaries <- lapply(quadratic_models, summary)

# Print summaries of each model
quadratic_summaries

7 Bonus question (20% pts)

For multiple linear regression, show that \(R^2\) is equal to the correlation between the response vector \(\mathbf{y} = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)^T\) and the fitted values \(\hat{\mathbf{y}} = (\hat y_1, \ldots, \hat y_n)^T\). That is \[ R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}} = [\operatorname{Cor}(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}})]^2. \]

7.1 Definitions:

  • Total Sum of Squares (TSS): This is the total variability in the response variable, which is defined as: \[ \text{TSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \bar{y})^2 \] where \(\bar{y}\) is the mean of the response vector \(\mathbf{y}\).

  • Residual Sum of Squares (RSS): This is the variability in the residuals (the difference between the observed and the fitted values), defined as: \[ \text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \] where \(\hat{y}_i\) is the fitted value for the \(i\)-th observation.

  • Explained Sum of Squares (ESS): This is the variability in the response that is explained by the fitted model. It is given by: \[ \text{ESS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2 \] The total variability in \(\mathbf{y}\) can be decomposed as: \[ \text{TSS} = \text{ESS} + \text{RSS} \] Thus: \[ R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}} \] This is the definition of $ R^2 $, the proportion of variance in $ $ that is explained by the fitted model.

7.2 Relationship Between Correlation and R^2

The square of the correlation between the response vector $ $ and the fitted values $ $ is given by: \[ [\operatorname{Cor}(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}})]^2 = \left( \frac{\text{Cov}(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}})}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(\mathbf{y}) \cdot \text{Var}(\hat{\mathbf{y}})}} \right)^2 \] where:

  • $ (, ) $ is the covariance between $ $ and $ $.
  • $ () $ is the variance of $ $.
  • $ () $ is the variance of the fitted values $ $.

However, since the model is linear, ( ) is the projection of ( ) onto the space spanned by the predictors. This means that ( ) has the same mean as ( ), i.e., ( {} = {y} ).

Thus, the covariance simplifies to: [ (, ) = _{i=1}^{n} (y_i - {y})(_i - {y}) ] which is just the explained sum of squares (ESS) divided by ( n ): [ (, ) = ]

7.6 Conclusion:

We have demonstrated that the coefficient of determination ( R^2 ), which is the proportion of variance in the response variable explained by the model, is equal to the square of the correlation between the observed response vector ( ) and the fitted values ( ).
